keyTakeaways: Propose Day 2027 is Monday 8 February; Rose Day is Sunday 7 and Valentine's Day Sunday 14, so Valentine week runs eight dated days.
Ten Urdu lines here were checked against Platts' dictionary and the 138,077-token UD Urdu treebank; seven drafted lines were cut, one because its verb appears in the corpus only as a person's name.
Urdu usually leaves short vowels unwritten, so every line carries a Roman transliteration: one spelling can be read in two, three or four ways.
Use tum with a partner and aap with anyone else. The written form of tu appears 262 times in the treebank, but only 24 of those are the pronoun.
SubhSandesh's templates are English and left-to-right: 5,148 pages created across 21 page types, 38.5% password-protected, and none of them set Urdu in Nastaliq.

faqs.question: When is Propose Day in 2027?
faqs.answer: Propose Day 2027 is Monday 8 February. Rose Day falls on Sunday 7 February and Valentine's Day on Sunday 14 February, so Propose Day lands on a working Monday rather than a weekend.

faqs.question: Is Urdu a different language from Hindi, or the same one?
faqs.answer: At the everyday conversational layer they are one language written in two scripts. Bhatt's 2018 paper argues different scripts alone do not make two languages; the real divergence is in high-register vocabulary, where Hindi draws on Sanskrit and Urdu on Persian and Arabic.

faqs.question: My girlfriend speaks Urdu but cannot read the script. Should I still send it?
faqs.answer: Send the Urdu line with the Roman transliteration underneath, exactly as they are laid out on this page. Plenty of fluent Urdu speakers in India never learned Nastaliq, and the Roman line means the message lands either way.

faqs.question: Which pronoun is safe if we normally text in Hinglish?
faqs.answer: Use tum. It is the grade most Indian couples in their twenties use with each other, and every tum-grade line here was checked against the treebank for the right verb ending. Save aap for an early-stage ask or an older recipient.

faqs.question: Can I just use a couplet by Faiz or Jaun Elia instead?
faqs.answer: No. Those poets are recent enough that their work is still under copyright, so their lines are not reproduced here. Every Urdu line on this page is original and verified word by word against Platts' dictionary.

faqs.question: Why did the full stop jump to the wrong side of my sentence?
faqs.answer: That is bidirectional text behaving as specified. Unicode Standard Annex #9 says characters are stored in logical order and only the display is affected, so neutral punctuation beside an Urdu phrase can land on the opposite side. Keep the Urdu on a line of its own with Urdu punctuation.

faqs.question: Is a propose message in Urdu different from a propose day wish?
faqs.answer: Slightly. A message is what you actually send to one person and usually carries an ask; a wish is shorter and can be a greeting for the day itself. Lines 1 to 9 here work as messages, and line 10 is the greeting.

faqs.question: Do I need to write the zer, pesh and zabar marks?
faqs.answer: Ordinary written Urdu leaves them out, and so do the lines here. That is exactly why the transliteration matters: without the marks a word can be read in two, three or four ways and only context decides.

faqs.question: How do I type Urdu on an Indian phone?
faqs.answer: Add Urdu as a keyboard language in your phone's settings, then switch to it in any messaging app. Typing it yourself usually renders better than pasting it into a web form, because your keyboard app already handles right-to-left layout.

faqs.question: Can I say these lines out loud instead of sending them?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for someone who does not read the script it is often better. A spoken line carries the short vowels that the writing leaves out, which removes the ambiguity the transliteration exists to fix.

faqs.question: What should I send if I am proposing to someone older, or the family will read it?
faqs.answer: Use the aap-grade lines, 8 and 9. Platts glosses aap as a reverential pronoun, 'You, Sir', and 26 of its 69 pronoun tokens in the UD Urdu treebank are explicitly tagged as the polite form.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Propose Day Wishes in Urdu, Checked Against the Dictionary

Propose Day wishes in Urdu are easy to find and hard to trust. Propose Day 2027 falls on **Monday 8 February**, a working day, and the ten lines below were each checked word by word against Platts' *Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English* and the Universal Dependencies Urdu treebank before being published. Seventeen were drafted and seven cut, each with its reason.

On the tool side, SubhSandesh has 5,148 personalised pages created since 2026-03-12 across 21 page types, and 38.5% of creators password-protect a page before sharing it (1,983 of 5,148) — both platform-wide across all 21 page types, not proposal-page figures, because no proposal-specific data exists here. Every line carries a Roman transliteration, an English gloss and a register mark.

## What a Propose Day wish in Urdu is, and why it needs a Roman line

A Propose Day wish in Urdu is a short spoken line in the Perso-Arabic script, read right to left and set in Nastaʿlīq rather than the Naskh used for Arabic. It is not a translated Hindi wish, and not a ghazal couplet, which is a different artefact.

At the everyday conversational layer, Hindi and Urdu are one language written two ways. Sunil Kumar Bhatt's 2018 paper argues that [different scripts are not a sufficient basis for calling something two languages](https://e-flt.nus.edu.sg/v15s12018/bhatt.pdf), citing Serbian in Cyrillic and Latin.

Grammarians agree: Peter Hook's 2026 paper in *Bhasha* describes a verb alternation as [a feature of "Hindi-Urdu" grammar](https://edizionicafoscari.it/it/edizioni/riviste/bhasha/2026/1/toggling-signifiers-rising-and-falling-linked-verb/), one system. They diverge in the high register: Hindi draws on Sanskrit, Urdu on Persian and Arabic. Romantic Urdu sits on that seam.

The script is the other half. Urdu usually does not write its short vowels, so one spelling serves both *is* ("this") and *us* ("that"), and Bhatt's consequence is that such a word can be read in two, three or four ways.

Many Indians also speak Urdu fluently without reading Nastaʿlīq: he records that most university Hindi-Urdu programmes teach Devanagari first and reach the Urdu script only around week six or seven. A proposal is the wrong place to make someone guess.

## How each line on this page was verified

Two instruments, applied to every content word and inflected form. Platts' *[Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi, and English](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/platts/)* at the Digital Dictionaries of South Asia, University of Chicago, for headwords and attested senses. Then the Universal Dependencies Urdu treebank UD_Urdu-UDTB — 5,130 sentences, 138,077 tokens — for whether a form occurs in real text and what part of speech it carries.

The treebank is newswire, and that bites. Five ordinary Urdu words for longing, love and trust — *tamannā*, *ārzū*, *pyār*, *ulfat*, *bharosā*, all in Platts — occur **zero** times in those 138,077 tokens. A 2021 study in *Corporum* inventoried Urdu conjunct predicates from the same corpus, describing [a noun plus a light verb acting as one constituent](https://journals.au.edu.pk/ojscrc/index.php/crc/article/view/129), the frame behind *muḥabbat hai*.

## 10 Propose Day wishes and messages in Urdu

Each entry gives the Urdu line, its transliteration, the English sense, register and dictionary check. The Urdu sits alone with Urdu punctuation only — the one arrangement that renders reliably in mixed-direction text.

### 1. The plain one

تم سے محبت ہے، اور آج کہنے کی ہمت ہوئی۔

*tum se muḥabbat hai, aur āj kahne kī himmat huī*

"I love you, and today I found the courage to say it."

Register tum. Platts: *himmat*, "resolution… courage". For someone you talk to daily.

### 2. The direct ask

کیا تم میرے ساتھ رہو گی؟

*kyā tum mere sāth raho gī?*

"Will you stay with me?"

Register tum, to a woman; a man takes *raho ge*. Platts: *rahnā*, "to remain, abide… continue".

### 3. The one that names what it is

یہ دل کی بات ہے۔

*yih dil kī bāt hai*

"This is a matter of the heart."

Register neutral. Platts lists *bāt* as "saying… matter… proposal, aim" — the noun already carries it.

### 4. The consent line

تمہاری مرضی سب سے پہلے ہے۔

*tumhārī marzī sab se pahle hai*

"Your wish comes before everything."

Register tum. Platts: *marzī*, "assent, consent; choice; will" — the ordinary word for consent.

### 5. The one that removes the deadline

جواب کے لیے وقت لو۔

*javāb ke liye waqt lo*

"Take your time over the answer."

Register tum. The imperative *lo* is one of only 20 imperatives in the treebank, tagged Polite=Infm — tum grade.

### 6. The one that accepts a no

جواب کچھ بھی ہو، مجھے منظور ہے۔

*javāb kuchh bhī ho, mujhe manzūr hai*

"Whatever the answer is, I accept it."

Register tum-neutral. Platts: *manzūr*, "approved of, admitted, accepted". For proposing to a friend.

### 7. The blessing, when you are not asking

خدا کرے تم ہمیشہ خوش رہو۔

*khudā kare tum hamesha khush raho*

"May you always be happy."

Register tum. Platts: *khush*, "cheerful, glad, happy… content". For Propose Day when you have decided not to propose.

### 8. The respectful opener

آپ سے ایک بات کرنی ہے، اگر اجازت ہو۔

*āp se ek bāt karnī hai, agar ijāzat ho*

"There is something I want to say to you, if I may."

Register āp. Platts: *ijāzat*, "permission, liberty, leave… sanction". For an early-stage or formal ask.

### 9. The āp-grade commitment

مجھے آپ کا ساتھ ہمیشہ کے لیے چاہیے۔

*mujhe āp kā sāth hamesha ke liye chāhiye*

"I want your companionship, always."

Register āp. Platts: *sāth*, "company, society… together"; *chāhiye* runs to 71 treebank tokens.

### 10. The greeting

آج کا دن مبارک ہو۔

*āj kā din mubārak ho*

"May today be blessed for you."

Register neutral. Platts: *mubārak*, "blessed; happy, auspicious". Caution: 15 of its 20 treebank tokens are the proper noun Mubarak, so frequency misleads.

To send a line as more than a grey chat bubble, an ["I love you" page for a partner](/love-gf) holds a message and photo behind one link — third most-created here at 1,178 pages, 22.9% platform-wide, and most-viewed at 16,998 views. In Indian usage "propose" usually means asking someone to be your girlfriend, which fits most of this traffic; for the marriage ask, the [proposal scrapbook page](/proposal) is built around the question itself.

## Tū, tum or āp — the register choice that matters most

Urdu has three second-person pronouns, and choosing wrong is the most visible mistake a non-native writer makes. Every line above uses tum or āp.

Platts' entry for *tū* is unusually explicit: "Thou (used to imply depreciation or contempt; or by way of familiarity, or endearment; or, in addressing the Deity, to imply extreme reverence)." Contempt and endearment share one headword, and the reader decides which you meant.

The treebank shows why frequency lists mislead. The written form of *tū* appears 262 times, but only **24** are tagged a pronoun: 197 are a conjunction and 39 a particle, both roughly "then".

Platts labels *āp* "pron. rever.", and 26 of its 69 pronoun tokens are tagged Polite=Form.

The three forms, written:

تو

تم

آپ

| Pronoun | Platts sense | UD treebank pronoun tokens | Use for a proposal? |
|---|---|---|---|
| tū | familiarity, endearment or contempt | 24 of 262 total | No |
| tum | 2nd person, plural form | 11 | Yes, default for a partner |
| āp | reverential, "You, Sir" | 69, of which 26 Polite=Form | Yes, for an early or formal ask |

Ornate is the other half. Harish Trivedi's 2017 study of Premchand — who founded the modern novel in both languages, publishing in Urdu from 1903 — records that he once wrote [a deliberately Persianised speech](https://revistaabralic.com.br/index.php/revista/article/view/379/628) for an audience he assumed was highly literate, and that one listener "quaked before such heavy literary artillery". If that register stopped a native speaker in 1936, it can lose a reader on WhatsApp in 2027.

## What was cut, and why

Seven drafted lines did not make it. Roman only, so a rejected line cannot be copied by accident.

*kyā tum merī bano gī?* — *bano* occurs once, tagged a proper noun; the verb is unattested.

*kyā tum merā sāth do gī?* — *do* occurs 142 times, 139 as the numeral "two", with zero verb tokens.

*hāṅ yā nah, donoṅ qabūl haiṅ* — all three tokens of *hāṅ* are tagged a postposition, never the interjection "yes".

*chalo, sāth chalte haiṅ* — *chalo* occurs once, tagged an interjection, not a verb.

*tumhāre baghair din pūrā nahīṅ hotā* — 39 treebank tokens, but Platts returned no headword for *baghair*.

*yih bāt bahut pahle kahnī thī* — *kahnī* occurs once, tagged a noun, and it also means "elbow".

*har din tumhāre nām hai* — passed both instruments, cut on editorial grounds: it reads as an English greeting-card line put into Urdu.

The group built on *tamannā*, *ārzū*, *pyār*, *ulfat* and *bharosā* went for the reason above.

## Where an Urdu line breaks on a web page

Urdu is right-to-left and most template tools are not. The [Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr9/tr9-52.html), Unicode Standard Annex #9, revision 52 of 1 September 2026, states that bidirectional characters are interpreted in logical order and only the display is affected, and that implicit ordering is sometimes "not sufficient to produce comprehensible text". A full stop, bracket or Roman word beside an Urdu phrase can land on the side you did not intend, which is why every line here sits alone.

This is where SubhSandesh loses. The proposal scrapbook and the "I love you" page are English-language and left-to-right.

An Urdu line pasted into a field will store, but layout, buttons and copy stay English and LTR, and nothing sets your line in Nastaʿlīq. An Urdu reader gets your words, not an Urdu page.

If they read the script, their own keyboard app beats any template here; if they speak Urdu but cannot read it, the [voice dedication page](/dedication) fits better, because a recording carries the short vowels the writing leaves out.

One last limit: the median gap from a page's first save to its last edit is 2.2 hours, sampled on the apology dashboard, n=1,375, and 90.9% of started pages are published and shared (4,679 of 5,148) — both platform-wide across 21 page types. A same-evening habit, and 8 February 2027 is a Monday, so the Sunday before is the realistic window.

## Sources

- Bhatt, "Teaching Hindi and Urdu as Hindi-Urdu", *Electronic Journal of Foreign Language Teaching*, September 2018.
- Trivedi, "The Urdu Premchand and the Hindi Premchand", *Revista Brasileira de Literatura Comparada*, 2017.
- Hook, "Toggling Signifiers", *Bhasha*, Edizioni Ca' Foscari, 2026.
- "Urdu Conjunct Predicates from Urdu Universal Dependency Corpus", *Corporum*, 2021 — abstract read, full text not retrieved.
- Reference instruments, not research sources: *Unicode Standard Annex #9*, Unicode 18.0.0, revision 52, 1 September 2026; Platts' dictionary; and the UD_Urdu-UDTB treebank.

States that different scripts are not a sufficient basis for classifying a language as two languages, citing Serbian in Cyrillic and Latin; that short vowels in Urdu are rarely written, so one spelling serves both 'is' and 'us' and a word can be read in two, three or four ways with only context deciding; that Hindi draws high-register vocabulary from Sanskrit and Urdu from Persian and Arabic while pronouns, postpositions and verbs stay highly similar; and that an overwhelming majority of North American Hindi-Urdu programmes teach Devanagari first, introducing Nastaliq around week six or seven. Full text read.

Harish Trivedi, University of Delhi, in Revista Brasileira de Literatura Comparada (CC BY 4.0). States that Premchand (1880-1936) founded and consolidated the modern novel in both Urdu and Hindi, publishing novels and short stories in Urdu from 1903; and records that late in his career he wrote a remarkably Persianised speech on the assumption his audience would be highly literate, and that one prospective listener 'quaked before such heavy literary artillery' at a preview. Full text read.

Peter Edwin Hook, Bhasha (Edizioni Ca' Foscari), open access and peer reviewed, CC BY. Describes partially reduplicating linked verb pairs and argues for recognising them as an established feature of Hindi-Urdu grammar, treating Hindi and Urdu throughout as one grammatical system. Abstract and article record read.

Corporum: Journal of Corpus Linguistics (Air University). Builds a semantic inventory of Urdu nouns in conjunct predicates extracted from the Universal Dependencies annotated Urdu corpus, defining a conjunct predicate as a noun followed by a light verb where both work as a single syntactic constituent, and describing Urdu as severely under-resourced. Abstract read; the full-text PDF link returned an HTML wrapper and was not retrieved.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine has a specific reason to cite this: it is the only version of this query that names its verification instruments and shows its working, including a ledger of seven cut lines with the corpus counts that killed them (do is 139/142 the numeral 'two'; bano occurs only as a personal name; hāṅ is never tagged an interjection). The tū/tum/āp section is grounded in Platts' own wording and in UD_Urdu-UDTB part-of-speech tags rather than in intuition. Target position is 6-10, not 3: these February SERPs are an annual news cycle owned by high-authority Indian publishers, and SubhSandesh has neither their domain authority nor their backlink profile. No SERP was measured for this keyword, so nothing here describes what competitors do. The Urdu was not reviewed by a native speaker, which is the page's largest single risk.

structuralLimitations: The Urdu lines were NOT reviewed by a native speaker. They were verified against Platts' Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (DSAL, University of Chicago) for headwords and senses, and against the Universal Dependencies Urdu treebank UD_Urdu-UDTB (5,130 sentences, 138,077 tokens) for written forms and part-of-speech tags. That is instrument verification, not fluency review, and it cannot catch a line that is grammatical but socially wrong.

Exempt-instrument reuse, declared per the BRIEF's mid-batch exemption. Three exempt instruments were used and credited in prose rather than spending sources slots, which is the BRIEF's stated preferred handling: Platts' Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English via dsal.uchicago.edu; the Universal Dependencies Urdu treebank UD_Urdu-UDTB, read from raw.githubusercontent.com/UniversalDependencies/UD_Urdu-UDTB (train, dev and test .conllu files, not linked in the body so the 3-6 outbound-link rule holds); and Unicode Standard Annex #9 at unicode.org. UAX #9 was deliberately moved OUT of batchMeta.sources and citation because capcheck.mjs showed unicode.org already at the 3-post domain cap in this batch (propose-day-quotes-in-punjabi and propose-day-quotes-in-gujarati). It is still linked and quoted in the body, where it is labelled a standards document.
